about.note: The Town of Tamworth, Carroll County, includes Tamworth Village, Chocorua, South Tamworth and Wonalancet. It is run by a five-member Select Board (Board of Selectmen) with a Town Administrator; officers and ordinances are voted by ballot at the annual Town Meeting in March (March 10, 2026). The town posts minutes in its online Agenda Center, but for this research only the April 14, 2026 Select Board minutes, the June 23, 2026 nonpublic session minutes, one Planning Board set (March 25) and one Capital Improvement Plan Committee set (September 16) could be opened. Other Select Board minutes posted through October 13, 2026 could not be opened, so meeting coverage is thin and some entries come from town notices and the Conway Daily Sun. The 2026 town warrant and MS-636 budget form are scanned files that could not be read; budget figures come from the town's 2026 draft budget. Plain-English summaries written by AI; items with needs_review=true are uncertain.

issues.title: Four-way stops in Chocorua (Routes 16 and 113) and Tamworth Village
issues.status: On hold: the state Department of Transportation (NHDOT) paused the Chocorua four-way stop in June 2026 to review a corridor study first
issues.summary: NHDOT offered to add four-way stops at several intersections on Route 113. In April the Select Board asked for one at Routes 16 and 113 in Chocorua and for turning the Tamworth Village three-way stop into a four-way stop. In June NHDOT said it had decided not to do the Chocorua project for now.
points: March 2026: NHDOT engineers proposed four-way stops at Routes 113 and 16, Route 113 and Page Hill Road, and Route 113 at 113A and Main Street (Conway Daily Sun).
NHDOT counted 23 crashes at the Chocorua intersection over about ten years, 18 involving more than one vehicle (Conway Daily Sun).

April 14: the board voted 4-1 (Schaeffer no) to send NHDOT a letter supporting the Chocorua stop, on condition that NHDOT reviews it within a year of construction and the town keeps working on better speed limit signs.

April 14: the board voted 4-1 (Prentice no) to ask NHDOT to make the Village three-way stop a four-way stop, leaving the slip lane as is. The Tamworth Village Safety Committee had recommended waiting for a larger engineering project.
The Chocorua Village Association supported the Route 16/113 stop but not one at Page Hill Road; the board did not request Page Hill.

June 23: at a listening session with about 60 people, the board was told NHDOT had "decided not to do the project." The NHDOT commissioner said the state wants to review the corridor study and all options first; Executive Councilor Kenney said the study could take a couple of years.
Town Administrator Nolan said the board could pay for the study from budget funds without a special town meeting (Conway Daily Sun).

issues.title: Required building notification (Regulatory Compliance Ordinance)
issues.summary: Voters adopted a Regulatory Compliance Ordinance at the March 10, 2026 Town Meeting. It makes building notification required again and sets up an application for a certificate of regulatory compliance, so town officials learn when a project needs Planning Board or Select Board review under rules the town already has.
points: Supporters said it adds no new land use rules; it is a way to tell officials when work, such as a driveway permit, earth excavation or a subdivision, triggers existing rules (Citizen Portal summary of the January hearing).

Voters approved a building notification form in 2004, but it was later made voluntary because it had been adopted under the wrong state law; the town gets about 80 voluntary notifications a year (same summary).
The draft carried over a $5,000 project threshold from the old form; presenters said it could be clarified as the form and fee schedule are written.
After the public hearing, the Select Board voted by voice to put the ordinance on the March ballot, with no recorded opposition.
April 14: a job description for a Regulatory Compliance Officer was due to come to the Select Board in May.
The ordinance and the 2026 Building Notification Form are posted on the town website; questions go to the Town Administrator, 603-323-7515 x14.

issues.title: Transfer Station rebuild and the new recycling center
issues.status: Recycling center fully open (September 2026); ribbon cutting was set for September 29
issues.summary: A 2022 Town Meeting vote approved major improvements to recycling at the Transfer Station, 550 White Mountain Highway (Route 25). The station now has new equipment and a dedicated recycling building, which opened in September 2026. Part of the cost was planned to be covered by a federal U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) grant.
points: Dec 22, 2025: the board approved buying a backhoe, a new compactor and four 45-yard containers, with delivery contingent on USDA reimbursement from a grant of up to about $493,000 (Citizen Portal summary).
At a meeting summarized March 7, 2026, the board let the Transfer Station Improvement Committee keep helping with bids and project delivery through the end of the year (Citizen Portal summary).
April 14: construction of the recycling building had started; a high water table might require raising it slightly.
April 14: the board voted, all yes, to send about a dozen food and beverage businesses a letter asking them to separate glass and aluminum, because trash tonnage costs the town double.
September 15: the town announced the recycling center was fully open after a soft opening, with aluminum and cardboard already being baled.
The 2026 draft budget lists $352,656 for the Transfer Station, up from $330,961 in 2025.

issues.title: Public electric vehicle charger at the Town Office
issues.status: Approved for construction September 9, 2026; ribbon cutting expected mid to late October
issues.summary: Voters approved an electric vehicle (EV) charger project at the March 2026 Town Meeting. The Energy Committee raised the money from private donations, and the Select Board approved moving it into construction on September 9.
points: One dual-port Blink Level 2 pedestal charger at the back of the expanded parking lot paved as part of the Tamworth Community Nurses Association (TCNA) building project.
Paid for with 50 private donations totaling $22,651 from seven businesses and organizations, 43 households and two in-kind donors; TCNA also paid about $5,000 for trenching and conduit.
Local and donated labor cut costs by about $4,000. Power use will be managed through the Town Office electrical panel.
Next steps listed in September: order equipment, pour a concrete pad, install and test, set up payment, then a public ribbon cutting.
Questions: TamworthEnergy@TamworthNH.gov.

issues.title: Updating the 2008 Master Plan, starting with housing
issues.status: Planning Board work under way; the board is seeking an interim member and an alternate
issues.summary: Tamworth's Master Plan (the long-range plan that guides zoning) dates from 2008. The Planning Board began updating it in 2026, starting with the housing chapter, with help from the Lakes Region Planning Commission (LRPC). It is also revising its subdivision rules.
points: March 25: the board discussed forming a Master Plan committee with substantial public participation; most of the work was expected in the fall. Members were asked to read the housing chapter before May 13.
April 14: the Select Board heard that the Planning Board's May 13 work session would start the Master Plan with housing, with an LRPC team attending.
A Master Plan survey flyer is posted on the Planning Board page.
Subdivision regulation changes under discussion include the definition of a "site" (which needs a legal opinion) and new major and minor subdivision categories.
October 14: the board is seeking an interim member (term to March 2027) and an alternate; contact Chair Elsa Weintraub at pbchair@tamworthnh.gov.
The Planning Board meets the fourth Wednesday of the month at 5:30 PM.

issues.title: Capital Improvement Program and the 2027 budget
issues.status: Capital Improvement Plan Committee approved its plan September 16; it went to the Planning Board September 23 and the Select Board October 13
issues.summary: Each year a town committee updates the Capital Improvement Program (CIP, a schedule of big purchases and savings for them) ahead of the next Town Meeting. The 2026 draft budget cut capital spending sharply from 2025 and used no surplus to lower taxes.
points: Sept 16: the CIP Committee approved the plan unanimously after a public hearing; Nick Grant was to present it to the Planning Board on September 23 and Chair Kathi Padgett to the Select Board on October 13.
The 2026 draft budget lists $347,320 for capital improvements, down from $1,308,976 in 2025.
The draft lists $157,000 for the fire truck capital reserve (warrant article 5) and $150,000 for the bridge capital reserve (warrant article 6).
The draft used $0 from fund balance (town savings) in 2026, compared with $611,514 in 2025, and estimates $3,243,606 to be raised by taxes, up from $2,535,752.
Tamworth's 2025 total tax rate was $14.78 per $1,000: town $3.37, local school $9.59, state education $1.09, county $0.73 (NH DRA).

issues.title: School tax cap question on the November 3 ballot
issues.next: 2026-11-03: State general election, K.A. Brett School gymnasium, 8 AM to 7 PM
issues.summary: A new state law (HB 1300, Chapter 324) puts a question on the November 2026 and November 2028 ballots asking whether to cap the local school tax. It also caps school central office administrative costs. SAU 13, which serves Tamworth, Madison and Freedom, has posted explainers.
points: SAU 13 says the question goes on the ballot automatically, bypassing local warrant articles and town meeting votes.
SAU 13 posted four explainers: what the tax cap law is, what is in the budget, local control and costs, and unintended consequences.
The local school share was $9.59 of Tamworth's $14.78 tax rate in 2025, about 65 percent (NH DRA).

The draft was read through a text extraction, and its printed 2026 total ($5,168,684) differs by $2 from the sum of its lines. The warrant, MS-636 and Town Meeting results could not be read.
